EMANCIPATION OF A MINOR — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Sam T. Rivera · June 12, 2010

MINOR'S DECLARATION AND BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR A PROSPECTIVE EMANCIPATION PETITION
I, Sam T. Rivera, was born on June 12, 2010. I am gathering background information for use with a prospective petition for a declaration of emancipation under California's Emancipation of Minors Law, Family Code §§ 7110-7123, to be filed, if at all, in the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County. So far as known, my parent(s) or guardian of record are Taylor M. Rivera and Casey L. Nguyen, where applicable. This declaration is background information only. It is not itself a petition, does not commence a court proceeding, and does not emancipate me or determine that I meet the statutory requirements a court would have to find before issuing a declaration of emancipation. Only a court, after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process described in this document's accompanying authority clauses, can issue that declaration.

INFORMATION SUMMARY — PROSPECTIVE PETITION FOR A DECLARATION OF EMANCIPATION
This information sheet summarizes background information regarding a prospective petition for a declaration of emancipation for Sam T. Rivera, born June 12, 2010. If a petition is filed, California law directs that it be filed in the superior court of the county in which the minor resides or is temporarily domiciled — here identified as the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County. So far as known, Sam T. Rivera's parent(s) or guardian of record are Taylor M. Rivera and Casey L. Nguyen, where applicable; California's notice statute would require them, or proof that their addresses are unknown, to be given notice before any hearing on the petition. This information sheet does not itself determine whether Sam T. Rivera satisfies the statutory eligibility facts a petition must allege, does not file a petition, and does not emancipate any minor; the statutory framework governing eligibility, notice, the hearing, the legal effects of a declaration, and its possible voiding or rescission are described in this document's accompanying authority clauses.

THE EMANCIPATION OF MINORS LAW, AND THE THREE STATUTORY PATHS TO EMANCIPATED STATUS
California's Emancipation of Minors Law states that its purpose is to provide a clear statement defining emancipation and its consequences, and to permit an emancipated minor to obtain a court declaration of the minor's status. Under Family Code § 7002, a person under 18 is an emancipated minor if any one of three conditions is satisfied: the person has entered a valid marriage or established a valid domestic partnership, regardless of whether it has since been dissolved; the person is on active duty with the Armed Forces of the United States; or the person has received a court declaration of emancipation under Family Code § 7122. Only the third path involves the court petition process this document describes; the first two occur by operation of the statute itself, without any court filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is the purpose of this part to provide a clear statement defining emancipation and its consequences and to permit an emancipated minor to obtain a court declaration of the minor’s status."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7001 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7001 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7001.)
  "The person has entered into a valid marriage, or has established a valid domestic partnership, regardless of whether the marriage or the domestic partnership has been dissolved."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7002(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7002.)
  "The person is on active duty with the Armed Forces of the United States."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7002(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7002.)
  "The person has received a declaration of emancipation pursuant to Section 7122."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7002(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7002.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own statutory definition of emancipated status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's status, and not a claim that any specific minor has taken either of the non-judicial paths described here. This clause cites two sections: § 7001 (a single citation, standing alone) and § 7002, whose three subsections — § 7002(a), § 7002(b), and § 7002(c) — are all part of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source for the three-paths framework, not as three independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself emancipate any minor by any of the three paths it describes, and does not determine that any specific minor has married, entered a domestic partnership, entered active-duty military service, or received a court declaration.

WHO MAY PETITION, AND THE FACTS THE PETITION MUST ALLEGE
Family Code § 7120(a) allows a minor to petition the superior court of the county in which the minor resides or is temporarily domiciled for a declaration of emancipation. Under § 7120(b), the petition must set forth with specificity four facts: that the minor is at least 14 years of age; that the minor willingly lives separate and apart from the minor's parents or guardian with the consent or acquiescence of the minor's parents or guardian; that the minor is managing their own financial affairs, evidenced by a completed declaration of income and expenses on Judicial Council form FL-150; and that the source of the minor's income is not derived from any activity declared a crime under the laws of California or the United States.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A minor may petition the superior court of the county in which the minor resides or is temporarily domiciled for a declaration of emancipation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7120(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7120(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7120.)
  "The petition shall set forth with specificity all of the following facts: (1) The minor is at least 14 years of age. (2) The minor willingly lives separate and apart from the minor’s parents or guardian with the consent or acquiescence of the minor’s parents or guardian. (3) The minor is managing their own financial affairs. As evidence of this, the minor shall complete and attach a declaration of income and expenses as provided in Judicial Council form FL-150. (4) The source of the minor’s income is not derived from any activity declared to be a crime by the laws of this state or the laws of the United States."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7120(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7120(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7120.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the facts California law requires a petition to allege — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's situation. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7120(a) and § 7120(b)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself allege, verify, or determine that any specific minor — including a minor identified elsewhere in this document — actually satisfies any of these four statutory facts, is at least 14, lives apart from a parent or guardian with that parent's or guardian's consent, manages their own finances, or has a lawful source of income. Whether a particular minor's actual circumstances meet these requirements is a factual and legal question for the minor's petition and the court, not a determination this document makes.

NOTICE TO PARENTS, GUARDIAN, AND PUBLIC AGENCIES BEFORE THE HEARING
Before a petition for a declaration of emancipation is heard, Family Code § 7121(a) requires that notice the court determines reasonable be given to the minor's parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the minor's custody — or that proof be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that notice cannot otherwise be given. Under § 7121(b), the clerk of the court must also notify the local child support agency of the county where the matter will be heard, and, depending on the minor's status, the probation department if the minor is a ward of the court, or the county welfare department if the minor is a dependent child of the court. Section 7121(c) requires the notice to include a form by which the parents or guardian may consent in writing to the emancipation, together with a warning that a court may later void or rescind the declaration and that the parents may become liable for the minor's support and medical insurance coverage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Before the petition for a declaration of emancipation is heard, notice the court determines is reasonable shall be given to the minor’s parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the custody of the minor, or proof shall be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that for other reasons the notice cannot be given."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7121(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7121.)
  "The clerk of the court shall also notify the local child support agency of the county in which the matter is to be heard of the proceeding. If the minor is a ward of the court, notice shall be given to the probation department. If the child is a dependent child of the court, notice shall be given to the county welfare department."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7121(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7121.)
  "The notice shall include a form whereby the minor’s parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the custody of the minor may give their written consent to the petitioner’s emancipation. The notice shall include a warning that a court may void or rescind the declaration of emancipation and the parents may become liable for support and medical insurance coverage pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 4000) of Part 2 of Division 9 and Sections 17400, 17402, 17404, and 17422."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7121(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7121.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the notice California law requires before a petition is heard — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7121(a), § 7121(b), and § 7121(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself give notice to anyone, does not determine that notice to any specific parent or guardian named elsewhere in this document is required, excused, or has been given, and does not itself create any consent or liability the statute describes.

THE COURT'S FINDINGS, AND THE LEGAL EFFECT OF A DECLARATION
Family Code § 7122(a) directs the court to sustain the petition if it finds that the minor is a person described by § 7120 and that emancipation would not be contrary to the minor's best interest. Under § 7122(b), if the petition is sustained, the court must forthwith issue a declaration of emancipation, which the clerk of the court then files. Section 7122(c) makes the resulting declaration conclusive evidence that the minor is emancipated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The court shall sustain the petition if it finds that the minor is a person described by Section 7120 and that emancipation would not be contrary to the minor’s best interest."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7122(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7122.)
  "If the petition is sustained, the court shall forthwith issue a declaration of emancipation, which shall be filed by the clerk of the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7122(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7122.)
  "A declaration is conclusive evidence that the minor is emancipated."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7122(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7122.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the finding a California court must make and the legal effect of the resulting declaration — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7122(a), § 7122(b), and § 7122(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself find that any specific minor is a person described by § 7120, does not find that emancipation would or would not be contrary to any specific minor's best interest, and does not itself issue, and cannot substitute for, a court's declaration of emancipation.

WHAT EMANCIPATION CHANGES ONCE A DECLARATION IS GRANTED
Once emancipated — whether by court declaration or by one of the two other statutory paths — Family Code § 7050 treats the minor as an adult for a defined list of purposes. These include ending the minor's right to support from the minor's parents; ending the parents' right to the minor's earnings and to control the minor; the application of Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 300 and 601; and ending vicarious or imputed liability of the minor's parents or guardian for the minor's torts, subject to statutory exceptions for liability imposed by the Vehicle Code or arising from an agency relationship. Section 7050(e) also gives the minor an adult's capacity for a further, statutorily enumerated list of acts — among them consenting to medical, dental, or psychiatric care without parental consent, knowledge, or liability; entering a binding contract; suing or being sued in the minor's own name; establishing the minor's own residence; and enrolling in a school or college.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An emancipated minor shall be considered as being an adult for the following purposes: (a) The minor’s right to support by the minor’s parents. (b) The right of the minor’s parents to the minor’s earnings and to control the minor. (c) The application of Sections 300 and 601 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (d) Ending all vicarious or imputed liability of the minor’s parents or guardian for the minor’s torts. Nothing in this section affects any liability of a parent, guardian, spouse, or employer imposed by the Vehicle Code, or any vicarious liability that arises from an agency relationship."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7050(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7050(a)-(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7050.)
  "(e) The minor’s capacity to do any of the following: (1) Consent to medical, dental, or psychiatric care, without parental consent, knowledge, or liability. (2) Enter into a binding contract or give a delegation of power. (3) Buy, sell, lease, encumber, exchange, or transfer an interest in real or personal property, including, but not limited to, shares of stock in a domestic or foreign corporation or a membership in a nonprofit corporation. (4) Sue or be sued in the minor’s own name. (5) Compromise, settle, arbitrate, or otherwise adjust a claim, action, or proceeding by or against the minor. (6) Make or revoke a will. (7) Make a gift, outright or in trust. (8) Convey or release contingent or expectant interests in property, including marital property rights and any right of survivorship incident to joint tenancy, and consent to a transfer, encumbrance, or gift of marital property. (9) Exercise or release the minor’s powers as donee of a power of appointment unless the creating instrument otherwise provides. (10) Create for the minor’s own benefit or for the benefit of others a revocable or irrevocable trust. (11) Revoke a revocable trust. (12) Elect to take under or against a will. (13) Renounce or disclaim any interest acquired by testate or intestate succession or by inter vivos transfer, including exercise of the right to surrender the right to revoke a revocable trust. (14) Make an election referred to in Section 13502 of, or an election and agreement referred to in Section 13503 of, the Probate Code. (15) Establish the minor’s own residence. (16) Apply for a work permit pursuant to Section 49110 of the Education Code without the request of the minor’s parents. (17) Enroll in a school or college."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7050(e) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7050(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7050.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the legal effects California law attaches to emancipated status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's status. Both citations in this clause are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 7050, subsections (a)-(d) and (e)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. An earlier research assumption in the task brief framed the effects provisions as falling within Family Code §§ 7120-7143; on the actual statutory text, the effects of emancipation are instead set out in a separate chapter, §§ 7050-7052 (Chapter 2, "Effect of Emancipation"), which precedes the court-declaration procedure in §§ 7110-7143 (Chapter 3) and is not part of the range the brief identified — this clause corrects that gap. This document is informational only: it does not itself confer any of these effects on any specific minor, and describes them only as consequences the statute attaches to a person who has actually become an emancipated minor under § 7002 — not as a statement that any specific minor identified in this document has become emancipated.

VOIDING A DECLARATION FOR FRAUD, AND RESCINDING ONE FOR INDIGENCY
A declaration of emancipation is not necessarily permanent. Family Code § 7130(a) makes a declaration obtained by fraud or by withholding material information voidable, while § 7130(b) makes a declaration of an indigent minor with no means of support subject to rescission — two distinct grounds, each with its own standard. Under § 7131, a petition to void a declaration for fraud or withheld information may be filed by any person or by any public or private agency, in the court that issued the declaration. A petition to rescind a declaration for indigency, by contrast, may under § 7132(a) be filed only by the minor, the minor's conservator, or the district attorney of the county where the minor resides, and must be filed in the county where the minor or conservator resides; § 7132(b) lets the court treat a minor as indigent if the minor's only income is public assistance benefits, and requires the court to find that rescission would not be contrary to the minor's best interest before granting it. Before either kind of petition is heard, § 7133(a) requires notice the court determines reasonable to the minor's parents or guardian, or proof that notice cannot be given. Finally, § 7135 provides that voiding or rescinding a declaration does not alter any contractual obligation, right, or property interest that arose while the declaration was in effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A declaration of emancipation obtained by fraud or by the withholding of material information is voidable."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7130(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7130(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7130.)
  "A declaration of emancipation of a minor who is indigent and has no means of support is subject to rescission."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7130(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7130(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7130.)
  "A petition to void a declaration of emancipation on the ground that the declaration was obtained by fraud or by the withholding of material information may be filed by any person or by any public or private agency. The petition shall be filed in the court that made the declaration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7131 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7131 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7131.)
  "A petition to rescind a declaration of emancipation on the ground that the minor is indigent and has no means of support may be filed by the minor declared emancipated, by the minor’s conservator, or by the district attorney of the county in which the minor resides. The petition shall be filed in the county in which the minor or the conservator resides."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7132(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7132(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7132.)
  "The minor may be considered indigent if the minor’s only source of income is from public assistance benefits. The court shall consider the impact of the rescission of the declaration of emancipation on the minor and shall find the rescission of the declaration of emancipation will not be contrary to the best interest of the minor before granting the order to rescind."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7132(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7132(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7132.)
  "Before a petition under this article is heard, notice the court determines is reasonable shall be given to the minor’s parents or guardian, or proof shall be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that for other reasons the notice cannot be given."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7133(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7133(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7133.)
  "Voiding or rescission of the declaration of emancipation does not alter any contractual obligation or right or any property right or interest that arose during the period that the declaration was in effect."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7135 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 7135 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7135.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a California declaration of emancipation may later be voided or rescinded — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific declaration. Two pairs of these citations are subsections of the same statutory section and are each treated as one source rather than independently corroborating sources: § 7130(a) and § 7130(b) (the two grounds), and § 7132(a) and § 7132(b) (the rescission-petition procedure and standard). Section 7131, § 7133(a), and § 7135 are each drawn from separate, independently numbered sections. This document is informational only: it does not itself void, rescind, or otherwise affect any declaration of emancipation, and does not determine that any specific declaration was or was not obtained by fraud or that any specific minor is or is not indigent within the meaning of § 7132(b).

HOW EMANCIPATION AFFECTS AN EXISTING GUARDIANSHIP OF THE PERSON
California's guardianship-termination statute cross-references the Emancipation of Minors Law directly. Probate Code § 1600(b) provides that a guardianship of the person terminates upon the death of the ward, the adoption of the ward, or upon the emancipation of the ward under Section 7002 of the Family Code — meaning an existing guardianship of a minor's person ends once that minor becomes an emancipated minor within the meaning of Family Code § 7002, by any of that section's three statutory paths, and not only through the court-declaration path this document otherwise describes. Probate Code § 1600(c) addresses termination of a guardianship of the estate separately, on its own terms, and does not list emancipation among the events that terminate a guardianship of the estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A guardianship of the person terminates upon the death of the ward, the adoption of the ward, or upon the emancipation of the ward under Section 7002 of the Family Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1600(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1600.)
  "A guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1600(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1600.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's guardianship-termination statute treats emancipation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1600(b) and § 1600(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. No separate statutory provision was located that bars a court from being asked to appoint a new guardian for a minor who is already emancipated, or that otherwise addresses guardian eligibility specifically in light of a minor's emancipated status; this clause describes only the one express cross-reference this research located — automatic termination of an existing guardianship of the person under § 1600(b) — and does not assert a broader rule beyond that text. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any guardianship, and does not determine that any specific minor named elsewhere in this document, or any guardianship concerning that minor, is affected by § 1600(b).

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — EMANCIPATION INFORMATION SHEET

Executed on April 1, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

expectedJSON.body: Before a petition for a declaration of emancipation is heard, Family Code § 7121(a) requires that notice the court determines reasonable be given to the minor's parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the minor's custody — or that proof be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that notice cannot otherwise be given. Under § 7121(b), the clerk of the court must also notify the local child support agency of the county where the matter will be heard, and, depending on the minor's status, the probation department if the minor is a ward of the court, or the county welfare department if the minor is a dependent child of the court. Section 7121(c) requires the notice to include a form by which the parents or guardian may consent in writing to the emancipation, together with a warning that a court may later void or rescind the declaration and that the parents may become liable for the minor's support and medical insurance coverage.

expectedJSON.body: Once emancipated — whether by court declaration or by one of the two other statutory paths — Family Code § 7050 treats the minor as an adult for a defined list of purposes. These include ending the minor's right to support from the minor's parents; ending the parents' right to the minor's earnings and to control the minor; the application of Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 300 and 601; and ending vicarious or imputed liability of the minor's parents or guardian for the minor's torts, subject to statutory exceptions for liability imposed by the Vehicle Code or arising from an agency relationship. Section 7050(e) also gives the minor an adult's capacity for a further, statutorily enumerated list of acts — among them consenting to medical, dental, or psychiatric care without parental consent, knowledge, or liability; entering a binding contract; suing or being sued in the minor's own name; establishing the minor's own residence; and enrolling in a school or college.

citations.quote: An emancipated minor shall be considered as being an adult for the following purposes: (a) The minor’s right to support by the minor’s parents. (b) The right of the minor’s parents to the minor’s earnings and to control the minor. (c) The application of Sections 300 and 601 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (d) Ending all vicarious or imputed liability of the minor’s parents or guardian for the minor’s torts. Nothing in this section affects any liability of a parent, guardian, spouse, or employer imposed by the Vehicle Code, or any vicarious liability that arises from an agency relationship.

(2) Enter into a binding contract or give a delegation of power. (3) Buy, sell, lease, encumber, exchange, or transfer an interest in real or personal property, including, but not limited to, shares of stock in a domestic or foreign corporation or a membership in a nonprofit corporation. (4) Sue or be sued in the minor’s own name. (5) Compromise, settle, arbitrate, or otherwise adjust a claim, action, or proceeding by or against the minor. (6) Make or revoke a will. (7) Make a gift, outright or in trust. (8) Convey or release contingent or expectant interests in property, including marital property rights and any right of survivorship incident to joint tenancy, and consent to a transfer, encumbrance, or gift of marital property. (9) Exercise or release the minor’s powers as donee of a power of appointment unless the creating instrument otherwise provides. (10) Create for the minor’s own benefit or for the benefit of others a revocable or irrevocable trust. (11) Revoke a revocable trust. (12) Elect to take under or against a will. (13) Renounce or disclaim any interest acquired by testate or intestate succession or by inter vivos transfer, including exercise of the right to surrender the right to revoke a revocable trust. (14) Make an election referred to in Section 13502 of, or an election and agreement referred to in Section 13503 of, the Probate Code. (15) Establish the minor’s own residence. (16) Apply for a work permit pursuant to Section 49110 of the Education Code without the request of the minor’s parents. (17) Enroll in a school or college.

expectedJSON.body: A declaration of emancipation is not necessarily permanent. Family Code § 7130(a) makes a declaration obtained by fraud or by withholding material information voidable, while § 7130(b) makes a declaration of an indigent minor with no means of support subject to rescission — two distinct grounds, each with its own standard. Under § 7131, a petition to void a declaration for fraud or withheld information may be filed by any person or by any public or private agency, in the court that issued the declaration. A petition to rescind a declaration for indigency, by contrast, may under § 7132(a) be filed only by the minor, the minor's conservator, or the district attorney of the county where the minor resides, and must be filed in the county where the minor or conservator resides; § 7132(b) lets the court treat a minor as indigent if the minor's only income is public assistance benefits, and requires the court to find that rescission would not be contrary to the minor's best interest before granting it. Before either kind of petition is heard, § 7133(a) requires notice the court determines reasonable to the minor's parents or guardian, or proof that notice cannot be given. Finally, § 7135 provides that voiding or rescinding a declaration does not alter any contractual obligation, right, or property interest that arose while the declaration was in effect.

expectedJSON.body: California's guardianship-termination statute cross-references the Emancipation of Minors Law directly. Probate Code § 1600(b) provides that a guardianship of the person terminates upon the death of the ward, the adoption of the ward, or upon the emancipation of the ward under Section 7002 of the Family Code — meaning an existing guardianship of a minor's person ends once that minor becomes an emancipated minor within the meaning of Family Code § 7002, by any of that section's three statutory paths, and not only through the court-declaration path this document otherwise describes. Probate Code § 1600(c) addresses termination of a guardianship of the estate separately, on its own terms, and does not list emancipation among the events that terminate a guardianship of the estate.
